title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-serving, Observability, Performance
author: Michael Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure as code, model-serving conventions, observability, and performance SLOs. It is intended for all engineering teams building services that run on or integrate with the Redwood inference platform.

Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated and private product components, customer-facing APIs, internal control-plane services, and model-serving runtime components. Excludes one-off experimental prototypes (these should be promoted to conforming design if they graduate).

Principles (high level)
- Developer-first: APIs and configs must be discoverable, well-documented, and ergonomically consistent.
- Production-ready by default: design for operability, monitoring, and secure defaults.
- Cost-aware: prefer patterns that give predictable unit economics (batching, caching, quantization).
- Safe rollout and observable change: every production change must include rollout strategy, monitoring and rollback plan.

1) API Standards
Intro: All public and internal HTTP/GRPC APIs should follow the contract below to reduce integration cost and ensure consistent behavior across services. Use OpenAPI (v3) for REST endpoints and protobuf for gRPC.

A. Endpoint & Versioning- Use explicit versioning in path: /v1/, /v2/ for breaking changes.
- New non-breaking features are released behind feature flags for at least 30 days before version bump.

B. Resource naming and paths- Use plural nouns for resources (e.g., /models, /deployments).
- Use hierarchical paths for containment (e.g., /projects/{project_id}/models).

C. Authentication & Authorization- All endpoints require auth. Public hosted API: token-based Bearer (short-lived token recommended for SDKs).
- Internal service-to-service: mTLS or short-lived service tokens issued by platform IAM.

D. Request/Response format- Prefer JSON for REST; use application/json; charset=utf-8.
- Use consistent envelope for errors: {
  "code": "string",
  "message": "human-friendly message",
  "details": []
}
- Streaming API: use chunked HTTP with server-sent events or gRPC streaming for large/long-running responses.

E. Error handling and retries- Return clear 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors.
- Include idempotency guidance in API docs.
- Retry policy: callers may retry on 503 and 429 with exponential backoff and jitter; do not retry on 4xx other than 429.

F. Pagination & Rate limiting- Cursor-based pagination preferred for large result sets.
- Expose rate limit headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

Example OpenAPI snippet (illustrative):
```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
paths:
  /v1/models:
    post:
      summary: Create model entry
      security:
        - bearerAuth: []
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/CreateModelRequest'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Created
        '400':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/BadRequest'
```

2) Coding Standards
- Languages & frameworks: Python (data/ML tooling), Go (control plane & runtime orchestration), TypeScript (frontend & API gateway helpers).
- Linters and formatters required: black/isort/flake8 for Python, golangci-lint for Go, eslint & prettier for TypeScript.
- Commit policy: small focused commits, descriptive commit messages, link to PR/issue.
- Tests: unit tests for logic, integration tests for external interactions, end-to-end smoke tests for critical flows. Coverage: target >= 70% for new services; critical libraries target >= 85%.
- Code review: at least one peer review + one approver from owning team. Security-related changes require security review.
- Dependency policy: use dependency scanning (Snyk/Dependabot) and schedule dependency upgrades at least quarterly.

Repository layout (recommended)
- /cmd (Go binaries)
- /pkg (reusable packages)
- /internal (private packages)
- /api (OpenAPI or protobuf)
- /deploy (deployment manifests)

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC & cloud)
- IaC: Terraform (v1.4+) is the standard for cloud infra. Keep modules small and documented.
- State: remote state in locked S3 backend with DynamoDB locking.
- Secrets: do not store secrets in Git. Use KMS + Secrets Manager or customer KMS for private deployments.
- Networking: use clear tagging and VPC/subnet patterns; services must support regional failover.
- CI/CD: pipelines must run unit tests, static analysis, build artifacts, run integration tests, and apply via Terraform in a gated promotion pipeline.
- Environment parity: dev -> staging -> prod promotion with invariant deployment manifests and separate parameterization for credentials/limits.

IAM & Access controls- Principle of least privilege; service principals scoped to resources.
- Use roles for cross-account access for Private deployments.

4) Model-serving Standards
Goal: Ensure models served by Redwood are consistent, efficient, and predictable across deployments.

A. Packaging & Artifacts- Models must include: model weights, tokenizer/vocab, config metadata (architecture, supported sequence length, quantization profile), and an inference contract (API schema).
- Supported formats: ONNX, PyTorch (.pt/.bin), or Redwood-verified quantized packages (.rwdq).

B. Quantization & Performance Profiles- Each model artifact must include a quantization profile indicating supported formats (fp16, int8, dynamic quant). Include expected throughput and latency at reference hardware.

C. Kernel selection & compatibility- Runtime chooses kernels based on model architecture and sequence distribution; model packaging should include preferred kernels and fallbacks.

D. KV Cache & Prefix Caching- Models exposing caching-friendly behavior must document cacheable prefix lengths and tokenization boundary expectations.

E. Routing, fallback & variants- For latency/cost tradeoffs, publish a set of compatible variants (e.g., gpt-like-large-fp16, gpt-like-large-int8). Smart routing policies will fallback to compatible variant if primary is constrained.

F. Rollouts & A/B testing- Default rollout strategy: staged canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with 30 minutes observation per step and automated rollback on error budget or quality regression.

Deployment checklist (before promoting a model to production)
1. Artifact validation (checksums, signature).
2. Performance benchmark on representative hardware (P50/P95/P99).
3. Quality benchmarks with evaluation prompt-set; ensure no regression beyond threshold.
4. Observability hooks (metrics, logs, traces) instrumented.
5. Canary rollout plan + rollback playbook documented and tested.

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics: expose Prometheus metrics with consistent naming: redwood_<service>_<component>_<metric> (e.g., redwood_runtime_inference_latency_ms).
- Required metrics: request_count, success_count, error_count (5xx/4xx), token_count, batch_size, latency_p50/p95/p99, cache_hit_rate, gpu_utilization.
- Tracing: use W3C Trace Context headers. All critical request paths must have traces captured; sample rate default 10% for high-volume paths, 100% for canaries and failures.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_id (if present), message.
- Dashboards: every service must publish a per-route dashboard showing latency, errors, token throughput, cost estimate.

Alerting & SLOs- Standard SLO template: availability, latency, correctness (quality regressions). Configure burn-rate alerting using error budget windows.

6) Performance Standards & SLOs
- API latency SLOs (hosted control plane & public endpoints):
  - P50 <= 100ms
  - P95 <= 300ms
  - P99 <= 800ms
- Model inference SLOs (per-token on reference hardware; values illustrative\u2014set per-model during onboarding):
  - baseline-small: P95 <= 10ms / token
  - baseline-medium: P95 <= 25ms / token
  - baseline-large: P95 <= 60ms / token
- Throughput & concurrency: define safe concurrency and target batching windows. Default batching guidance: aim for <= 50ms max queuing to preserve latency SLOs.
- Error budget policy: 4-week rolling error budget; automated degradations/fallbacks when budget consumed beyond threshold.

Performance testing requirements
- All new services and model variants must run performance tests against the benchmarking suite (see bench/ in runtime repo) before production. Include steady-state and spike scenarios.

7) ADRs and Decision Records
- Format: ADR-YYYYMMDD-<short-title>. Use consistent metadata: status, context, decision, consequences, owners.
- Canonical ADRs (examples):
  - ADR-20240215-runtime-kernel-selection: Choose runtime-driven kernel selection for optimized latency across histograms.
  - ADR-20240601-quantization-policy: Adopt int8 dynamic quantization as default for cost-sensitive workloads with per-model opt-in.
- When an ADR impacts user-facing behavior (API or SLA), note it in release notes and notify downstream teams.

8) Governance, Review & Exceptions
- Standards owner: Architecture Council (rotating chairs from eng-platform & runtime).
- Review cadence: quarterly standards review; ad-hoc for critical gaps.
- Exceptions: must be documented with mitigation, TTL, and approval by Standards owner and Security if applicable.

9) Operational runbook pointers (summary)
- Incident detection: use SLO burn-rate alerts -> oncall page -> runbook.
- Common mitigations: scale up dedicated pools, switch to fallback model variant, enable degraded mode (turn off heavy evals/costly logs).

10) Appendix: Sample Canary Rollout Procedure (model variant)
1. Validate artifact signature and checksums.
2. Deploy to canary pool (tagged) at 5% traffic.
3. Run smoke calls for functional correctness and run eval prompts.
4. Monitor key metrics for 30 minutes: latency (P95), error_rate, quality_score (eval).
5. If metrics stable, increase to 25% for 30 minutes.
6. If stable, increase to 100%. Otherwise rollback to previous variant and open postmortem.
